Chapter 4: How Belief in God Can Be Rational
Picture this: in a quiet library, a philosophy major is hunched over a pile of thick books, trying to untangle the arguments for and against belief in God. The deeper he dives, the more complicated it all seems. Some writers claim that faith is irrational—a relic from a less enlightened time. But others say belief in God isn’t just reasonable; it’s actually necessary if you want to make sense of life itself. Stuck between these two worlds, the student feels lost, unsure which path to choose.
If you’ve ever found yourself wrestling with these big questions, you’re definitely not alone. It’s tough for anyone who wants to take both faith and reason seriously. The real issue isn’t just whether believing in God feels comforting—it’s whether you can defend that belief when the tough questions come up. So many people think being rational means you should only believe what can be proven beyond all doubt. But here’s something to pay attention to: that standard is impossible, not just for faith, but for pretty much everything we believe.
Think about how you trust your own mind. Most of us never stop to wonder if our thoughts are reliable, or if the world outside our heads is actually real. But these are assumptions we can’t strictly prove. Philosophers have pointed out that everyone relies on what they call “basic beliefs”—convictions we just accept, without proof, because we need them to make sense of anything at all.
Now, some argue that belief in God is one of these basic beliefs. It isn’t necessarily the result of a long, complicated argument; instead, it’s a starting point—a foundation that helps us understand our experiences. Just like you trust your memory or believe other people exist without demanding absolute proof, you can see belief in God as a rational foundation for making sense of the world.
Imagine a young woman wrestling with doubt. She keeps circling back to a question that won’t let her go: why does anything exist at all? Sure, science can explain how things work, but it can’t answer why there’s something rather than nothing. The more she ponders it, the more she realizes that belief in God gives her a framework for these deep questions. It’s not about shutting down her mind—instead, it’s about opening it to possibilities that stretch beyond what we can measure or see.
This way of thinking is inspired by philosophers who say belief in God is “properly basic.” That means it doesn’t need to be justified by other beliefs—it stands on its own. But that doesn’t make faith arbitrary or immune to challenge. Like other basic beliefs, it can be rational to hold unless you run into a really strong reason to let it go.
Critics will often demand proof that God exists, but here’s the thing—they rarely hold their own beliefs to the same tough standard. Trust in reason, trusting your senses, believing that other people are real—none of these can be proven with absolute certainty, but we accept them anyway, because life just wouldn’t work otherwise. So the real question isn’t whether belief in God can be proven beyond doubt. It’s whether that belief helps you make sense of the world in a way that’s coherent and satisfying.
There’s a story about a philosophy professor who once challenged his students to doubt everything. But instead of finding clarity, they just got stuck—paralyzed, unable to move forward. Turns out, even the most skeptical person has to start somewhere. For many people, belief in God isn’t a crutch—it’s a foundation. It’s a way of making sense of life that’s both rational and deeply human.
